private.note: Private, so it can't be in the index: there is no daily price to track. Followed here through the valuation at each funding round. If it goes public, it gets screened like everyone else.

leader.line: Born in Iran. Fled to Sweden at six. Co-founded Databricks.
leader.story: Ali Ghodsi was born in Iran in 1978. His family fled to Sweden when he was six, where he grew up and earned a PhD in distributed systems at KTH. As a visiting scholar at UC Berkeley he helped create Apache Spark, co-founded Databricks in 2013, and has run it since 2016.

holdings.name: Intuit

leader.line: Arrived from Tehran at nine. Engineer. CEO of Intuit since 2019.
leader.credit: Photo: Intuit Corp., CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
leader.story: Sasan Goodarzi came to the United States from Tehran at nine, during the revolution, and finished high school in Orlando. An electrical engineer with a Kellogg MBA, he worked at Honeywell and Invensys, joined Intuit in 2004 and became CEO in 2019.

holdings.thesis: Sasan Goodarzi has run Intuit since 2019: TurboTax, QuickBooks, Credit Karma, Mailchimp. Top-tier software margins, and the stock has been cut way down this year. That's why it has the best value score in the index.

holdings.name: Teledyne Technologies

leader.line: Born in Tehran. MIT doctorate. Led Carnegie Mellon, then Teledyne.
leader.story: Robert Mehrabian was born in Tehran in 1941 and earned his bachelor's and doctorate at MIT. A materials scientist, he was president of Carnegie Mellon University from 1990 to 1997, then led Teledyne as CEO from its 1999 spin-off through 2018. He has been Executive Chairman since 2019.

holdings.thesis: Robert Mehrabian was born in Tehran and ran Teledyne as CEO from its 1999 spin-off through 2018, turning it into a buy-and-build machine for sensors, cameras and defense electronics. He has been Executive Chairman since 2019. Steady growth, real free cash flow, and a long record of smart acquisitions.

holdings.name: Uber Technologies

leader.line: Born in Tehran. Ran Expedia for 12 years. Made Uber profitable.
leader.story: Dara Khosrowshahi was born in Tehran in 1969. His family left as the revolution began and rebuilt in New York. After Brown, he spent twelve years running Expedia, then took over Uber in 2017 and turned a company losing billions into one that makes money.

holdings.thesis: Dara took over in 2017 when Uber was burning billions a year. It now makes real money and throws off free cash. He's a hired CEO, so it scores low on founder skin. It's in for the business, and the size of it.

holdings.name: Prologis

leader.line: Left Tehran at 14. MIT at 16. Built the world's largest logistics landlord.
leader.story: Hamid Moghadam left Tehran at 14, finished school in Switzerland and arrived at MIT at 16. After a Stanford MBA he co-founded AMB in 1983, and in 2011 merged it with ProLogis to create the largest logistics real estate company in the world. He became Executive Chairman in 2026.

holdings.thesis: Hamid Moghadam co-founded Prologis in 1983 and built it into the biggest warehouse landlord in the world. He handed the CEO job to Dan Letter in January 2026 and stays on as Executive Chairman. Huge, steady cash flows, and the AI data-center build-out is a new tailwind for its land.

holdings.name: Biglari Holdings
holdings.thesis: Sardar Biglari founded Biglari Holdings: revenue up 8% on the year, a 8% operating margin. Scores 63 on quality, 49 on catalysts and 54 on rerating room, out of 100.

holdings.name: Life Time Group

leader.line: Left Tehran at 17. Bet everything on one club in 1992.
leader.story: Bahram Akradi left Tehran at 17 in 1978, worked in restaurants to pay for an electrical engineering degree at the University of Colorado, and found his way into the health-club business. In 1992 he sold everything he owned to open one club in Brooklyn Park, Minnesota, a site where three clubs had already failed. That club became Life Time.

holdings.thesis: Bahram Akradi founded Life Time in 1992 and still owns a big piece of it. Profitable and growing, but it carries the most debt of the four and is spending heavily on new clubs, so free cash flow is negative for now. That keeps it at the minimum weight.

holdings.name: Precigen
holdings.thesis: Helen Sabzevari leads Precigen: revenue up 6323% on the year, a 41% operating margin. Scores 36 on quality, 65 on catalysts and 44 on rerating room, out of 100.

schemes.name: PRSN method
schemes.note: Score only, no size, momentum, 5–20% limits

conclusions: Weighting: Same, no momentum had the best risk-adjusted return (Sharpe 0.59). Our method ranks 2 of 7 at 0.57, after 10 bp trading costs.

Momentum: it made little difference over this period (Sharpe 0.57 with vs 0.59 without). Names in the top half on 12-month momentum beat the bottom half the next month 55% of the time, by +0.8 pts on average.

Trend: names above their 200-day average returned +2.8% the following month on average, vs +2.9% for names below it. That's no real edge, so the 200-day line is shown for context, not used in the weights.

Rebalancing: annual scored best (Sharpe 0.80), but the gaps between cadences are within noise for 57 months of data. Monthly plus a drift trigger keeps weights within 5 points of the rules and trades about 65% of the portfolio a year.
Macro: PRSN averaged +4.4% a month when the 10-year yield fell and -0.5% when it rose. It's a rate-sensitive basket.
Diversification: average correlation between holdings is 0.13 over the past year.

changelog.note: Launch. Six-factor score tilts an equal weight; 5-20% per name; monthly + 5-pt drift.
Quality first, then catalyst and rerate. Conviction tiers instead of equal weight. Small caps from $50M in a capped sleeve. Weekly checks; trades wait for a calm VIX.
